title: Code layout and line breaks
goal: Separate Ruby expressions clearly and continue an expression across lines.
paragraphs: Ruby treats a line break as the end of an expression when the expression is complete. A semicolon can separate expressions on one line, though separate lines are usually easier to read. Indentation helps people see structure; it does not replace Ruby's syntax.

Ruby can continue an expression when the current line is incomplete, such as after +. In that case the next line belongs to the same expression. Use parentheses or a clear line break to show how the parts fit together.
code:
first = 2
second = 3
total = first +
  second
puts total

experiments.title: Separate statements
experiments.task: Predict the two printed lines. Then put the assignments on separate lines without changing their values.
experiments.code:
first = 2; second = 3
puts first
puts second
experiments.answer: The semicolon separates the two assignments, so Ruby prints 2 and then 3. Moving each assignment to its own line keeps the same output and is easier to scan.

experiments.title: Continue an expression
experiments.task: What does total contain? Change the second addend from 3 to 8 and predict the new output.
experiments.answer: The plus sign leaves the expression incomplete, so the next line supplies its right-hand value. Changing 3 to 8 makes the output 18.

experiments.title: Use parentheses
experiments.task: This expression continues inside parentheses. Predict the result, then change 4 to 6. Does putting the grouped sum on separate lines change the calculation?
experiments.answer: The open parenthesis lets the grouped expression continue across lines. The result is 18; changing 4 to 6 makes it 24. Line breaks inside this grouping do not change the arithmetic.

pitfall: A line break after a complete expression starts a new expression. Put a continuation operator such as + at the end of the unfinished line, or use parentheses to make the grouping clear.
remaining: Backslash line continuation and optional separators in control structures are not covered.

title: Comments
goal: Add notes to Ruby code with comments that Ruby does not execute.
paragraphs: A comment begins with # and continues to the end of that line. You can put it on its own line or after Ruby code. Ruby ignores the comment text, so it does not change the program's output.
Use comments to explain a reason or intention that the code does not make clear. Keep executable Ruby outside the comment so the interpreter can run it.
code:
# Choose a value for the greeting
name = "Ruby" # this is a short comment
puts "Hello, #{name}!"

experiments.title: Comment out a line
experiments.task: Predict the output. Then remove the # before the first puts and predict both lines.
experiments.answer: Ruby ignores the first line because it starts with #. Removing that # makes the first puts run too, so both lines print.

experiments.title: Add an end-of-line note
experiments.task: What prints before the #? Change the number to 9 and predict the result.
experiments.code:
count = 4 # number of tries
puts count
experiments.answer: The text after # is a comment, so puts prints the assigned value 4. Changing the number to 9 makes it print 9.

experiments.title: Keep code outside the comment
experiments.task: Predict the output, then change "Ready" to "Done". Which text is part of the comment?
experiments.answer: Ruby runs puts and ignores the note after #. Changing the string changes the output to Done; the words after # still have no effect.

pitfall: Text after # on a line is a comment, including anything that looks like Ruby code. Put the code before # or on a separate line if it should run.
remaining: Block comments and magic comments are not covered.

title: Operators and precedence
goal: Group calculations deliberately and inspect comparisons.
paragraphs: Operator precedence determines how an expression groups its parts. Multiplication groups before addition. Parentheses make a different grouping explicit and can also make your intent easier to read.
== compares values; = performs assignment. Many Ruby operators are method calls on an object, so their behavior depends on the receiver. For example, + adds numbers but joins strings.
pitfall: The words and/or have different precedence from &&/||. Do not mechanically swap them in assignments.
remaining: Operator definitions on custom classes, bitwise operators, safe navigation and boolean assignment precedence need deeper treatment.

experiments.title: Compare the groupings
experiments.task: Compare the second calculation here with Example: why is its result 14 instead of 20?
experiments.answer: Here 3 + 4 is grouped before multiplying by 2, giving 14. Example groups 2 + 3 first and then multiplies by 4, giving 20.

experiments.title: Compare two expressions
experiments.task: Why do the expressions produce different totals?
experiments.answer: Multiplication groups before addition unless parentheses change the grouping.

experiments.title: Join strings
experiments.task: Change second to " rules". What does + do here?
experiments.answer: For strings, + joins the receiver and argument into a new string.
